John the Apostle. One of Jesus's twelve apostles, traditionally known as "the beloved disciple" for his closeness to Jesus. He was present at the Last Supper, reclining next to Jesus, and was entrusted with the care of Jesus's mother Mary. He witnessed the Crucifixion and was at the empty tomb on the Resurrection morning. John is traditionally credited with authoring the Gospel of John, which presents Jesus's ministry with theological depth and poetic language unlike the other Gospel accounts. He also wrote three epistles known as 1, 2, and 3 John, addressing faith, love, and eternal life. The Book of Revelation, an apocalyptic vision received while he was exiled on the island of Patmos, is traditionally attributed to him as well. Early church tradition holds that he lived to old age in Ephesus, making him the longest-lived apostle, and he shares his name with John the Baptist but is distinguished by his role as an apostle and his literary legacy in shaping New Testament theology.
